narrative_story:
# The Infinite Playoff

## I.

I work with a 0.5mm mechanical pencil, Pentel GraphGear 1000, because a finer point permits more legible notation in the margins of standard-issue scorecards, which allow approximately 3mm of usable annotation space between the pre-printed column dividers. I mention this because precision instruments matter. I mention this because the tools constrain the work and the work must be understood through its constraints.

My name is Gerald Maines. I hold a master's degree in applied statistics from the University of Delaware (2007, thesis: "Bayesian Correction Models for Heterogeneous Plate Discipline Metrics in A-Ball Environments"). I have been employed, in varying capacities, by four minor league organizations, two independent statistical consultancies, and, for the past nineteen months, by the Office of Competitive Integrity within the Atlantic Independent Professional Baseball Consortium, which oversees the operational and financial compliance of six affiliated leagues comprising forty-one active franchises across the Mid-Atlantic and southeastern regions.

I was hired to investigate irregularities in the 2022 and 2023 seasonal records of the Delmarva River Dogs, an Advanced-A affiliate operating out of Salisbury, Maryland. The allegations, filed by an anonymous source within the league's umpiring corps, concerned possible point-shaving—specifically, the suspicion that certain games had been manipulated to produce outcomes favorable to regional betting lines. My mandate was narrow: examine the statistical record for anomalies inconsistent with natural game variance, flag any patterns suggestive of deliberate performance manipulation, and deliver a preliminary report within ninety days.

The work proceeds as follows. I obtain the official scorebooks—one maintained by the home team's scorer, one by the visiting team's, and one by the league-assigned official scorer. For each game under review, I reconcile these three records entry by entry: at-bat by at-bat, pitch sequence by pitch sequence where available, substitution by substitution. Discrepancies between the three are common and almost always trivial. A scorer in the home booth credits a hit; the league scorer rules an error. One book records a mound visit in the fourth; another places it in the fifth. These are the ordinary frictions of parallel human observation. I document each discrepancy in a reconciliation ledger—date, game number, inning, the nature of the divergence, the probable cause, and the resolution. Most resolve to scorer convention. A smaller number resolve to clerical error—transposed digits, skipped lines, ink smears on carbon copies. An even smaller number require judgment: was the third baseman's throw truly errant, or was Gutierrez's speed at first the determining factor? These I flag for secondary review and move on.

I am thorough. I have always been thorough. In my three years with the Hagerstown Suns organization (2013–2016), I reconciled 4,212 individual game logs and found a discrepancy rate of 1.7 percent, of which 94 percent resolved to the trivial categories above. I published a brief methodological note on the remaining 6 percent in the *Journal of Sports Analytics* (Vol. 4, No. 2, 2017, pp. 118–124), proposing a Bayesian reconciliation framework that weighted scorer reliability against contextual game factors. The note was cited eleven times. I do not mention this to boast. I mention it to establish that my process is documented, peer-reviewed, and reproducible. What I find, when I find it, is not a product of interpretation. It is a product of method applied to material. The method is sound. The material is what the material is.

I work in a windowless interior office on the second floor of the Consortium's administrative building in Columbia, Maryland. The room is eleven feet by nine feet—I measured it during my first week, not out of compulsion but because I was calculating whether the east wall could accommodate a second filing cabinet beside the existing shelving unit. It could, with four inches to spare. I requested the cabinet. It arrived in six weeks. It now contains the physical scorebooks for the 2022 Delmarva season, organized by date, home and away, each game in its own manila folder, each folder labeled in my hand with the Pentel 0.5mm in block capitals. The 2023 records are in the original cabinet. The database terminals—two, networked to the Consortium's central statistical repository—occupy the desk. A printer, laser, black-and-white only, sits on a stand I brought from home.

I list these things because they are what is here. They are what I work with. They are stable, physical, countable. The pencil, the cabinets, the records, the room. Eleven by nine.

I began in January. It is now March. I have reconciled 411 of the 548 total games played across both seasons. Of those 411, I have flagged 23 for secondary review—a rate of 5.6 percent, notably higher than the 1.7 percent baseline I established in Hagerstown. Seventeen of those 23 involve the River Dogs. That cluster is interesting. That cluster is what I was hired to find.

I have not yet found it.

What I mean is: the seventeen flagged games show elevated discrepancy rates, but the discrepancies do not pattern the way deliberate manipulation patterns. In a point-shaving scenario, you expect compression in late-inning scoring—narrowed margins in the seventh through ninth, sequences where the favored team approaches but does not reach the spread. The shape of the data is specific. I know the shape. I've modeled it. These seventeen games do not exhibit that shape. They exhibit something else.

I have not yet determined what.

---

## II.

The first anomaly I dismissed was in game 247, June 14, 2022, River Dogs at Fredericksburg Nationals, second game of a doubleheader. The Delmarva home scorer's book records Tyler Bascombe—River Dogs, number 34, right fielder—striking out looking to end the fifth inning, the 2-2 pitch a slider low and away, called by home plate umpire R. Dominguez. The league official scorer's book records the same at-bat: Bascombe, strikeout looking, 2-2 slider, Dominguez behind the plate.

The Fredericksburg visiting-team scorer's book records Bascombe hitting a ground-rule double to right-center on a 3-1 fastball in the same at-bat. Same game number, same inning, same batter, same lineup position. The pitch count is different. The outcome is different. The at-bat is, in two of three records, a strikeout, and in the third, a double.

I flagged the discrepancy as a probable scorer error—most likely a line-skip in the Fredericksburg book, where the scorer transposed the at-bat with one from a different game. This happens. Visiting-team scorers in the low minors are often volunteers, local journalists, retired coaches with inconsistent training. The explanation is sufficient. I coded the discrepancy as Class II (clerical, probable line-skip), noted it in the reconciliation ledger, and continued.

Game 251, June 17, 2022. Fredericksburg at River Dogs. All three scorebooks agree on every at-bat through the sixth inning. In the seventh, the home book records a pitching change: lefty reliever Marcus Cantu replaces starter David Flett. The visiting book records the same. The league book records no pitching change. According to the league scorer, Flett pitches the complete game—nine innings, 104 pitches, seven strikeouts, the line preserved in the Consortium's official database. According to both team scorers, Flett exits after six, Cantu pitches two, and closer Rodríguez finishes the ninth.

A database migration artifact. The Consortium transitioned from DataScore 4.1 to DataScore 5.0 in the 2022 offseason; game logs imported from the old system occasionally dropped mid-game substitution records. I had seen this in the Hagerstown data as well—the import script failed to parse multi-pitcher games where the substitution was recorded in a non-standard annotation format. I coded the discrepancy accordingly: Class III (systemic, database migration probable), noted it, continued.

Game 289. Game 307. Game 312. I began finding them every fifteen to twenty games, each one individually explicable, each explanation drawing from a different category of known error. A scorer's convention difference between a wild pitch and a passed ball. A game that appears in the River Dogs' seasonal record but not in the Lynchburg Hillcats' corresponding record, which I attributed to a scheduling amendment—Lynchburg had forfeited due to a travel cancellation, and forfeits are recorded by some teams as played games and by others as administrative entries. A player, José Medina, listed as the starting designated hitter for the River Dogs on July 23, 2022, while the Hillcats' records for the same date list J. Medina as pinch-hitting in the seventh inning of a concurrent game in Salem, Virginia. I checked and confirmed that there were two José Medinas in the Consortium system—one with the River Dogs, one with the Salem Red Sox, different middle initials, different jersey numbers. A common name. A minor indexing failure.

Each resolution held. Each resolution holds. I want to be clear about that. When I examine whatever single anomaly in isolation—pluck it from the sequence, set it under the light, turn it—the explanation is sound. Clerical error. Database artifact. Scorer convention. Homonymous players. The taxonomy of error is well-established and these are its standard species.

What I had not encountered before was this density. By the time I reached game 340, I had logged forty-one discrepancies across 298 reconciled games—a rate of 13.8 percent, more than eight times my Hagerstown baseline. Not all forty-one involve the River Dogs. Twenty-four do. The remaining seventeen are distributed across five other teams, including three involving Fredericksburg's records and two involving Salem's, which should not have appeared in the dataset at all since Salem falls outside the scope of my Delmarva investigation.

I expanded the scope. This was within my discretion under the terms of my mandate, which authorized secondary review of "any affiliated records relevant to the integrity determination." A discrepancy rate of 13.8 percent is relevant. I began reconciling non-Delmarva games, selecting them at random from the broader league schedule.

The rate held. Twelve to fifteen percent, regardless of the teams involved. In some cases higher.

I noted this in my working journal: *Discrepancy rate appears league-wide, not team-specific. Initial point-shaving hypothesis unsupported. Probable systemic data-quality issue in Consortium record-keeping infrastructure. Recommend comprehensive audit.*

This was on a Tuesday. I remember it was a Tuesday because I remember writing the date—March 4—and checking the calendar to confirm it fell within the third reconciliation cycle I had scheduled for myself, which ran Monday through Wednesday of each week. I remember the satisfaction of the note. It was clean. It diagnosed a problem, identified its scope, proposed a response. The investigation had not found what it was looking for, but it had found something, and the something was explicable—boring even, the way infrastructure failures are boring. A league that had grown too fast, added too many teams, staffed too many press boxes with undertrained scorers, and migrated its database carelessly. No conspiracy. No crime. Just entropy dressed in column headers.

I was not yet concerned.

The concern began on a Thursday—March 6—when I pulled the box score for game 401, August 19, 2022, the second game of a River Dogs–Fayetteville Woodpeckers series, and found that according to the Fayetteville scorer's book, the River Dogs' lineup included a player named Gerald Maines.

I do not play baseball. I have never played organized baseball. I have no connection to the Fayetteville Woodpeckers. My name—Gerald Maines—is not particularly common, but it is not unique. A search of the Consortium's player database returned no active or inactive player by that name. The Fayetteville book listed G. Maines batting eighth, playing second base, going one for three with a walk. No other scorebook for that game—home or league—included this name. In the home and league books, the eighth-place batter was R. Tejada, who went 0-for-4.

A coincidence of nomenclature, probably—a scorer mishearing a name over the PA system, or carrying a name from a roster sheet that had been incorrectly updated. In the low minors, roster turnover occurs weekly; a scorer working from a pre-printed lineup card might carry a ghost name for half a game before someone corrects it. I have seen this. It is, again, a known category.

But I did not code it. I set the page aside. I looked at it for longer than was useful.

Then I looked at the next set of games.

---

## III.

By the second week of March, the wall behind the filing cabinets was covered. I had purchased a roll of butcher paper—white, thirty-six inches wide—and taped it across the plaster in overlapping sheets, creating a single continuous surface approximately eleven feet by six feet. On this surface I had plotted the anomalies by date, team, and type, using a color-coding system: red for outcome discrepancies (a strikeout that was also a double), blue for existence discrepancies (a game that was also not a game), green for identity discrepancies (a player who was also a different player, or was also in a different city, or was also me). Pins connected related anomalies with thread. The thread was white, which in retrospect was a poor choice against the white paper, but by the time I realized this I had already strung so much of it that replacing it would have meant dismantling the entire map and starting over, which I could not afford to do because I had begun discovering things that existed only in the spatial relationships between the pins—patterns that were visible on the wall but that could not be reproduced in any list or database query I ran.

For instance: the identity discrepancies. There were now fourteen of them. In six, the phantom player appeared exclusively in the visiting team's scorer book. In five, the phantom appeared exclusively in the home team's book. In three, the phantom appeared in the league book and in one team book but not the other. When I plotted these fourteen games chronologically and drew connecting threads to the nearest outcome discrepancy (by date) and the nearest existence discrepancy (by date), the threads formed—this is difficult to describe, but I will describe it because precision is my instrument, precision is what I have—the threads formed a pattern in which each identity anomaly was bracketed, before and after, by one outcome anomaly and one existence anomaly, in alternating order, with a mean interval between them of 4.7 games, standard deviation 1.2.

This was not random. Or it was random and I was Pattern-seeking. But I had run a Monte Carlo simulation on my laptop—10,000 iterations, randomizing the positions of the anomalies across the 548-game dataset—and the observed bracketing pattern appeared in only 0.3 percent of simulated datasets. P-value: 0.003. That is significant. That is not the kind of number you get from noise.

Unless the simulation was wrong. Unless I had specified the pattern post hoc, which biases the significance test. Unless the anomalies themselves were not independent events, which violates the simulation's assumptions. The criticisms are obvious. I cataloged them. I did not resolve them.

What I want to describe now is the thing I found on March 11, because it is the thing that changed the investigation, though I no longer know into what.

Game 319, July 29, 2022. River Dogs at Lynchburg Hillcats. The home scorer's book for this game is a standard NCR triplicate carbon—white top sheet, yellow second, pink third—and the handwriting is neat, practiced, the work of someone who has scored hundreds of games. I had the white top sheet. The game it records is unremarkable through six innings: River Dogs leading 4-2, Hillcats threatening in the fifth but stranding runners, a rain delay of twelve minutes in the third. In the seventh, the Hillcats mount a rally. A single, a walk, a fielder's choice that advances the lead runner to third. Then the cleanup hitter, number 22, D. Washington, comes to the plate.

In the home scorer's book, Washington hits a sacrifice fly to center. Run scores. 4-3.

In the visiting scorer's book, Washington hits a sacrifice fly to center. Run scores. 4-3.

In the league scorer's book, Washington—number 22, D. Washington, same man, same at-bat—*pitches* to himself. He is listed as both the batter and the pitcher of record. The pitcher who had been on the mound through the first six innings—M. Paul
